The story of this course  Past → Patterns → Model → Forecast

Today’s learning outcomes  • Define a time series correctly • Explain why time order matters • Recognize real forecasting problems • Use notation Yₜ and forecast horizon • Separate signal, pattern, an
Motivation: public health forecasting  Question: Can we prepare beds, staff, and medicine for next week?  Time series helps us turn past weekly values into planned action.
Where do time series appear?  • Daily rainfall • Hourly electricity demand • Weekly dengue cases • Monthly sales • Stock or exchange rates
What is a time series?  A time series is a set of observations recorded in time order.  Y₁, Y₂, Y₃, …, Yₜ  The index t tells us WHEN the value was observed.

section_title: Not all data are time series
text: Not all data are time series  Many units  One unit many times  one time
Why does time order matter?  Because today may depend on yesterday.  Yₜ may depend on Yₜ₋₁, Yₜ₋₂, …  This dependence is the heart of time series analysis.

text: What patterns can hide inside a series?  • Trend: long-term movement • Seasonality: repeated calendar pattern • Cycle: irregular long wave • Noise: random variation

section_title: One Series Can Contain Many Stories
text: One Series Can Contain Many Stories  Observed value = signal + noise  Signal may include trend, seasonality and cycle.  Noise is what remains unexplained.
Component 1: Level and Trend  Level: Usual height.  Trend: Long-term direction.  Activity: Is baseline changing?
Component 2: Seasonality  Seasonality = fixed repeating calendar pattern. Rainfall often repeats within each year.  Question: What is the period?
Component 3: Cycle  Seasonality repeats on a known calendar.  Cycle repeats, but not with exact timing.  Examples:  • economic expansions and recessions  • disease waves  • consumer behaviour cycles
Component 4: Irregular Variation  Not everything is predictable.  Random shocks, recording errors, strikes, storms  and policy changes can disturb the pattern.
A good analyst asks:  “Is this noise, or is this a meaningful event?”

Additive Structure  Use when seasonal size is roughly constant.  Yₜ = Tₜ + Sₜ + Cₜ + Iₜ  Observed = Trend + Seasonal + Cycle + Irregular  Example: rainfall seasonal swing stays about  similar each yea
Multiplicative Structure  Use when seasonal size grows with the level.  Yₜ = Tₜ × Sₜ × Cₜ × Iₜ  Seasonal effect is proportional to the level.  Example: sales peaks become larger as business  grows.

WHAT Are the Components?  • Trend (T): long-term increase or decrease. • Seasonal (S): fixed repeating pattern. • Cycle (C): long waves without fixed calendar length. • Irregular (I): random unexplain

section_title: WHY Not Use Ordinary Correlation Only?
text: WHY Not Use Ordinary Correlation Only?  Ordinary correlation compares two different variables. Autocorrelation compares a series with its own past. Question changes from X vs Y to Yₜ vs Yₜ₋ₖ. This is

WHAT is a Lag?  Lag k means comparing Yₜ with Yₜ₋ₖ  Lag 1: today with yesterday. Lag 2: today with two periods ago. Lag 12 for monthly data: this month with same month last year.  DS5104 • Lecture 7 •

Lag-1 Relationship  Each point pairs a value with its previous value. Upward cloud means positive autocorrelation. Random cloud suggests little memory.  DS5104 • Lecture 7 • Autocorrelation & ACF • an

Theory: Autocovariance  γₖ = Cov(Yₜ, Yₜ₋ₖ)  It measures how values move together across lag k. Large positive γₖ: high values tend to follow high values. But covariance depends on the measurement unit

How to Interpret ρₖ  similar values repeat  ρₖ close to +1  little linear memory  ρₖ close to 0  high tends to follow low  ρₖ close to −1  DS5104 • Lecture 7 • Autocorrelation & ACF • anupama@foc.sab.
